utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Would the witness kindly take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I declare I will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Boering. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we move on to this witness, would you like to receive the motion concerning the notes of Colonel Rutten in writing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we do. Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel Boering.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you hear me in your language, in Nederlands?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I hear you perfectly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. First, I have just a couple questions about your testimony in the Popovic case. As I told you, we will be admitting -- seeking to admit that evidence rather than asking you all the same questions again today. Now, having reviewed your testimony in that case, can you confirm to the Trial Chamber that the transcript was accurate?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, in the past two weeks I reviewed the testimony again and I stand behind it entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And second question that I have to ask: If I were to ask you the same questions today on the same topics would you answer -- would your answers be the same? Would you give us the same information?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I assume I would provide virtually the same answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd seek to admit then that testimony which is 22421A, which would be under seal because it contains some private session, and 22421B, which would be the public version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What does the confidential part refer to, Mr. Nicholls? If necessary, we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: To be honest, Your Honour, I'm not sure exactly. I just -- we've been putting one in public and one in private. I could check that more carefully. I think there is some private session testimony in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit them both.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours the 65 ter 22421A will be Exhibit P3968 under seal and 65 ter 22421B will be Exhibit P3969.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll now read a summary of your testimony, sir. Colonel Boering arrived in Srebrenica on 3rd January 1995. At that time he held the rank of major and he served as the DutchBat liaison officer with the ABiH, the VRS, civilian leadership on the Serb and Muslim side, as well as the NGOs, such as MSF, Médecins sans Frontièrs, the ICRC, and UNHCR. In the course of his duties, he met with various VRS officers, including Drina Corps commander, General Zivanovic; Bratunac Brigade major, Momir Nikolic, with whom he met approximately every two weeks; and Skelani Brigade commander, Vukovic. And he also met with Colonel Beara twice. Colonel Boering also met with various ABiH officers in the enclave, including Naser Oric; Ramiz Becirovic; a person named Ekrem, a security officer; and Zulfo, who was an independent leadership in the Bandera triangle. And the witness would meet with an ABiH leader around about once a week. In his testimony, Colonel Boering described the mandate and deployment of DutchBat in the Srebrenica enclave, as well as his view of the structures of both the VRS and the ABiH. He described DutchBat's efforts to disarm persons with weapons inside the enclave and the difficulties. He described smuggling of weapons and helicopter flights into the enclave and complaints from the VRS about ABiH raids launched from inside the enclave to the outside against the Serb areas. Colonel Boering also described the poor humanitarian situation in the enclave and the deteriorating security situation in the months leading up to the VRS attack in July 1995. He described shortages of food, water, medical, and fuel supplies for the population, as well as problems with supplies that DutchBat had and how convoy restrictions affected the population and DutchBat. He testified that over the course of May, June, and July 1995 the intensity of shooting and shelling from the Serbian side into the enclave increased in this period. People were hurt and killed and their homes were shelled. He, himself, faced fire at his vehicle when leaving the UN compound to go on patrol in Potocari, and that the increasing fire from the VRS seriously hampered DutchBat's ability to go out and patrol. Regarding the fall of Srebrenica, Colonel Boering described the attack on Srebrenica, how in July the VRS took over UN observation posts and how some DutchBat soldiers were taken prisoner by advancing UN forces -- VRS forces, excuse me. The VRS fire at this time into the enclave caused more people to go to Srebrenica and seek shelter there, and the streets were overflowing with people. Boering described -- Colonel Boering described shelling by VRS that was close to the UN Bravo Company in Srebrenica and an incident where a little boy was injured by an explosion. He said the people looked -- the citizens look apathetic, hungry, and very nervous and asked the UN soldiers what would happen to them. On 10 July, when the situation became, in his words, hopeless, the population started moving towards Potocari and Colonel Boering went to Potocari with the people. He described the scene at Potocari where there were huge mass, thousands of people gathered around the UN compound there who were frightened and insecure. He testified that these people did not have enough food or water with them and that DutchBat could do very little because of their limited supplies. He estimated there were only enough supplies for a day or two. Coming to the Hotel Fontana meetings which the witness attended. Colonel Boering was present at all three meetings at the Hotel Fontana in Bratunac, which took place on the evening and night of 11 July, two meetings; and on the morning of 12 July, 1995. VRS representatives included Generals Mladic and Krstic and an officer the witness recalled as being named Kosuric or Kosovic and other VRS personnel and at the third meeting civilian personnel. Momir Nikolic was present at the start of all meetings, at least at the beginning. The witness testified that during the first meeting on 11 July, he and the others felt threatened. He recalled that Commander Karremans and DutchBat soldiers were physically pushed into the corner and that Mladic using threatening language and that Colonel Boering had to push back to get more room for DutchBat. He recalled that during the second Hotel Fontana meeting, that night, 11 July, an animal was slaughtered outside the meeting and the witness perceived this as an attempt to intimidate the DutchBat representatives present as well as the Muslim representative. The next morning, on 12 July, the witness attended the third meeting at the Hotel Fontana, and he was concerned about General Mladic's comments concerning the screening of all male refugees for possible war crimes. And the witness pointed out a civilian at the meeting who was tasked with that. Still on the 12th of July, after the meeting, Colonel Boering returned to Potocari. When he arrived he saw that Serb soldiers were preparing the boarding on buses of the people and their transport out of the enclave. He saw that Muslim men in Potocari were selected from the crowd and detained at the so-called "White House." Colonel Boering, himself, entered the "White House" and saw Muslim men sitting on the floor. Their documents were piled in a corner and at gunpoint Colonel Boering was ordered to leave the building by Serb soldiers, VRS soldiers. Colonel Boering testified that later -- he then later escorted a convoy of buses towards Tisca. In Tisca the convoy stopped. At this point he saw men from the convoy being separated, and these men - Muslim men who were taken off the buses, that is - and these men were taken away in the direction of the forest by VRS soldiers in the presence of Major Sarkic, who the witness knew, of the Milici Brigade. Colonel Boering could not follow these men to see what would happen to them. He was asked to walk with the women and children from Tisca through no man's land to the Muslim-held territories. He then escorted the women and children to safety. That concludes my summary. Now, Colonel, I'm just going to ask you a few questions to bring us up-to-date on your current situation and then I'll ask you about the third Hotel Fontana meeting. Could you tell the Trial Chamber what your profession is now. Are you still in the military?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I'm still in the military. I'm presently in Enschede at a school for co-operation between the military and civilians working with seven other countries specially focused on NATO training.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you tell me what your current rank is?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I'm -- my current rank is lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you described this school, but could you very -- just very briefly describe what your main duties are, in terms of what you've said about your current job.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: My duties, in fact, are that we do exercises, for example, deployment to Africa or a different crisis area; and then in the early stage there's co-operation with civilian organisations such as the UN and NATO and we plan how to set that up. And also how to elaborate the implementation, for example -- as happened, recently, for example, in Libya. That's at a higher level. At lower level in the field, there's co-operation between the Red Cross and other organisations, and in that area we perform trainings, both in Enschede and in the respective countries. We're also present at the training exercises and, if necessary, go to deployment areas such as Afghanistan to see how the training is proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now going to ask you just some questions about the third Hotel Fontana meeting on 12 July, and I'm going to watch the video with you. But before we get to that can you tell us just -- do you remember about what time that meeting started?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I think the meeting started at around 10.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just from your memory, who was there representing DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans was present and I was present for DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you remember, if you can, who was present from the Muslim population of Srebrenica side?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, there was Nesib Mandic and their representative of the women -- the first -- her first name was Camila, and the third man, Nuhanovic, probably was his last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And we'll see the video, but just from your memory, do you recall who was there from the VRS and Bosnian Serb civilian side?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Present from the VRS was General Mladic, General Krstic, Major Nikolic, Colonel Jankovic. And for the civilians, I don't remember the name exactly anymore, but if I watch the video I might remember. And there was somebody else present for the military responsible primarily for our removal and I'd have to see him to remember his name. That's all I remember for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And just to be very clear, I think we all know, but Major Nikolic, that's Major Momir Nikolic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to play the video if we could now, which is 65 ter 40582, part 2, which starts at 00:05:30 approximately. And, Your Honours, in the book which follows the video which is 65 ter 03099, this meeting is at pages 42 to 48, the stills. And when we play the video I think we may not need English interpretation over it because it has subtitles and you can hear the Serbian and Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, sir, I just ask you to look at the video. See if it helps you to remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could -- I'll ask Mr. Reid to play the video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The French booth has not been provided with a transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we stop for the moment. Did you hear the comment from the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honour. I'll see if we can have that e-mailed to them. And could we just go back to the video, Mr. Reid.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we stop, please. Go back one -- yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At 00:05:36.8, right at the beginning, sir, could you just tell us what this place is we see here in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: That's the entrance to Hotel Fontana, the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just if you can, can you tell us, if you remember, who are the four men we see in the frame, maybe starting left to right, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: At the left I see Major Momir Nikolic; next to him, Colonel Jankovic; next to him at the door I see General Mladic's body-guard; and I -- at this time I don't remember the man at the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We could play the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we stop there for one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The tall man in the camouflage T-shirt who drove the Muslim representatives to the meeting, who is that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: That's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. That was at 00:06:46.4. We can continue, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we make a stop?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that there's no -- there has been no French translation, but thanks to Judge Lattanzi we can continue. But I'm concerned about the French transcript later on. But in the meantime, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I apologise for that. We'll try in the future to make sure we have the French distributed for all of them. Continue, please, Mr. Reid.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We're at 00:13:09.4 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The man in the middle of the frame we see with, I'll say, the civilian open-collared shirt, do you remember at all what his role was, what you understood his role to be, why he was there?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: He'd been assigned a role, primarily to select potential war criminals among the Muslim population if they had to be selected.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that's -- in your previous testimony you referred to that as screening; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, it was screening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how did you learn that that was this man's role? How did -- who did you hear that from, or how did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: That came up at length at that third meeting in Fontana about how they expected to structure the age categories under his leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you remember how those age categories were to be structured, approximately?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I think not youths up to about 15 and not men from age 70 on. That's what was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be clear, this is talking about Muslim men in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we play the video, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop, please. We stopped at 00:15:08.6 where the video changes to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just a couple of follow-up questions, sir. The video we just watched is approximately ten minutes long. How long was the meeting [Realtime transcript read in error "video"] as you remember it?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I think at least half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we saw watching the video that it jumped a bit at some places as though it was cut or edited and we didn't see anywhere on the video the discussion of men being screened, of the process by which men would be screened for war crimes, which you said in your prior testimony General Mladic spoke about. Can you tell us, do you remember if the whole meeting was filmed or were only parts of it filmed?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: During that meeting, the film crew was present throughout and the scenes that I saw did not reflect the entire meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've described before how after the meeting you went back to Bratunac or -- sorry, you left Bratunac and went back towards Potocari and had a conversation with Commander Karremans, discussing you realised things were not entirely clear. And you went back to Bratunac. Could you just describe that to the Trial Chamber for us, that process.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The problem with the meeting in Bratunac was in part the language, even though I was sitting next to Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans and was sitting next to the interpreter and was translating softly for Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans what was being said. So I heard most of it but not everything. So the actual agreements about how to proceed, I had some gaps about that. That's why on the way back when we got back to Potocari, it was good to get together with Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans to hear what his findings were and to compare them with what I had heard. And it turned out that it was good to compare these because there was some confusion about the course of how to proceed and the commitments by Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans. For that reason, we decided that I would return to Bratunac to verify once again how we -- what the process would be from thereon and how we could assist in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I got in the car, I drove back to Bratunac, back to Hotel Fontana. And with a great deal of difficulty, eventually I found Major Momir Nikolic and asked to verify the status quo. And he indicated that I should leave as quickly as possible, that it was clear what would be happening, that's what he indicated, that I had to go back to Potocari. He was not happy that I appeared again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if I'm clear from your answer, he refused to discuss these issues with you?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, he refused to elaborate. He said, "You'll see, it's clear what the intention is."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions at this time, Colonel Boering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we deal with the associated exhibits -- before that, probably I have to ask Mr. Tieger. During yesterday we admitted the 65 ter 19458, which was the list of criminals, and due to time constraints I asked Ms. West as to its admission, but she -- I don't think she understood the question proceeded with different things and at the end of the day I admitted. My question is whether you do not object to the admission of that document? Do you remember what it is about?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me make sure I understand the Court's question. The question is not about the list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The list of criminals which was put by the accused to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, my -- I'll -- my understanding was that the issues -- that any issues pending -- that it was an MFI, of course, I recall. But as to the list, I thought I understood that Ms. West had not reserved an objection but had not made an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it was admitted in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I -- my question is: You do not challenge the authenticity of the document? That document is also one of the associated exhibits of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that was her intention and I didn't think she had any reservations to make with respect to that, but that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. First, I have to ask the Defence whether they have any objection to specific documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, I'd like to note down some -- seven documents about which I have some concerns about their nature as indispensable and inseparable part of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I can say too, Your Honours, and we can see if they overlap with yours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would agree. And that would be 19455, I -- on review it's not indispensable as well as 19471. Taking a look at that I thought there was not really much comment from the witness in the prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If I can identify further five. 19458, 19464, 19473, 19730, those are the documents put by the various Defence, but the witness was not able to answer any questions in a serious manner. And therefore I doubt whether -- if they form indispensable and inseparable part of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Therefore, if you would like to tender them, I would like you to deal with them; otherwise, the Defence may have to deal with them individually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If I can just take a quick look. I think 19458, unless my notes are wrong --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's the document I referred to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It was admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Admitted yesterday, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So I will skip that one. 19464, I will withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Nicholls, I omitted mentioning 19469 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I completely agree, Your Honours, starting with 19473.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, as we're going along here, I'm questioning the utility of this exercise because it's going to increase the time that we need for cross-examination. I'm wondering whether or not, given that there's no objection to these documents, although they didn't form an indispensable part of the testimony, whether they can nevertheless be admitted as agreed between the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we have a tool to admit such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It seems that it would be more efficient to do it that way, given that these were documents tendered by the Defence in the Popovic case and ones that we would like to have admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I meant, in that case, first, the Defence can put the questions in relation to these documents; otherwise, Defence -- it can use also bar table motion on the certain formalities. I'd like to stick to the principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I agree with Your Honour's remaining two, that they're not indispensable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. With that caveat, all the other associated exhibits will be admitted into evidence and be given a number in due course. Thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Lieutenant-Colonel Boering, as you heard, your evidence in the Popovic et al. case, i.e., its transcript has been admitted in full in lieu of your oral testimony. And now you will be further asked by Mr. Karadzic in his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Boering.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I would like to suggest that the time before the break -- actually, we can postpone the time before we begin because there's nobody to assist with the uploading. We need time to make it possible for my team to upload the documents or we can maybe do something else, but we don't have the option of spending the whole morning on uploading the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. I was trying to follow whether we can hear in Dutch, so I missed your submission. Let me read your transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you suggesting taking a break now? It's not clear from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, if the break will make it possible to do the uploading. It seems it's not just us who are short of staff, but it seems that the same would apply to the Registry as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for 20 minutes. We'll resume at quarter past. --- Break taken at 9.52 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Boering, how many statements in all did you provide?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, quite a few before this Tribunal, at least five times. Also to the NIOD, N-I-O-D, other statements, so probably about ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it correct that your first statement dates from September 1995, two months thus after your return to the Netherlands?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, do you mean a statement for the UN or domestically for the Netherlands?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To the Dutch authorities.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And that was the first statement, right, that you ever gave; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that statement, did you state all the characteristics, all the characteristic facts?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Every investigation and every question I was asked had a certain background and the first investigation also served a purpose. So specific questions were asked and each time I answered those.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to know, after that first statement, after your first statement that you provided to the United Nations, did you go for any kind of consultation?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: How do you mean that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you consult with anyone from the Dutch government in order to prepare for such a statement?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I don't remember the Dutch government preparing me for sessions such as this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you not state that after the first statement and before the second statement you visited the minister of defence and that you went over the documents with him; wasn't that so?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I remember that there was a difference between the statements that I compiled and what was, in fact, issued to the Tribunal, and I asked some questions about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection. I'm sorry to interrupt, but it's a recurring request. Could we please just have cites, at least to the statement if -- even if Mr. Karadzic isn't -- doesn't have his line references, at least when he says "didn't you state" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- it makes it much easier for me to follow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, I do have the right to put a question like this and to wait for the answer, and then depending on the answer I will see. Why would I indicate in advance what my intentions are? I'm interested to know whether that was so or not. I can say now that it was a statement from the 10th of February, 1998, that Mr. Boering provided. Now I'm going to look at this as 1D04718, so we can look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to briefly reply, Your Honour. I don't think Mr. Karadzic's characterisation of his right to ask questions without saying where they're coming from when they are put as statements of the witness as correct, he should -- and it's the convention in every other trial I've been in that when you say "you've said this," you give the cite to the opposing party and to the witness and to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's coming. Let us proceed. Bear that in mind, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, I didn't say you said that. I asked whether you went to consultations. And we have information in the statement that I just cited that Mr. Boering went to see the defence minister to go over documents and to refresh his recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you said "did you not state," in that case probably you need to cite the reference. Let's continue. We need to switch to e-court from Sanction. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your statement?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I see my signature and the date, yes, on the front page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3504 is what we need. That's the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the next page, please. Second paragraph. Would you please read it.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I'd like to get back to your previous question. This document does not apply to consultations with the Ministry of Defence; this is a UN investigation. So I assume that this is a new topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please read this paragraph. [In English] Would you like me to read it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have it. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to confirm that he went to see the minister and then I'm going to ask further what they discussed -- well, let's finish this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You went to see the minister for consultations during this visit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where do you have it, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I read it in English. "I would like to mention that on the second day of this interview I visited Dutch Ministry of Defence and reviewed documents to help refresh my recollection."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where did he say he met minister, Mr. Karadzic, and consult him?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The ministry, the ministry. I don't know how this was translated to you, the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, having read that paragraph, please proceed your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you get information at the time about what happened to the film that was taken by your associates in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: No, I did not receive any information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know why these films were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I don't know whether those films were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will remind you that the person who made the films, who took the films, stated in his initial statements that he handed the films over to the intelligence officer, to somebody from the intelligence service, and that in the later statements he said that they were destroyed. However, he said that he was told that those films were much more accusatory or inculpatory than they expected and they told him that he should not talk about the films at all. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I know Mr. Rutten, but I was unaware that he wasn't allowed to talk about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just for the record, we haven't been told which precise statement, again, that Mr. Karadzic is talking about from Mr. Rutten, but the proposition put to the witness misstates the evidence given yesterday at page 30, line 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. I was about to put that question to you as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I had had enough time, Your Excellencies, I would have confronted the witness with his earlier statement -- I mean yesterday's witness. He said that: [In English] "All of the conversations with Rutten held on 18th -- 19th of August, 1992, document 06054891 to 0605482 -- 024, page 4."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll just say it's incredible not to confront the witness yesterday with that proposition under the excuse of no time when the witness yesterday said exactly what happened to the film, which was different, and then try to use this witness to get in the alternate theory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I can't agree more, Mr. Nicholls. But do you not challenge that such statement existed? Because I'm not -- we are not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't have it in front of me, Your Honours. It may have been notified, but I haven't seen it yet. I don't at this point challenge that he's reading from something correctly. My point was it should have been put to the witness yesterday so that he could explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is really difficult to follow, Mr. Robinson. If you could give Mr. Karadzic advice after this -- after this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I will. But I can't help but take this opportunity to note that if we had had adequate time to prepare for this portion of the case we could work out some of these problems. I can tell you, really, from working inside this team that the preparation for the Srebrenica part of the case is woefully inadequate and these things will happen time and time again since we don't have enough time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, but I can't accept the explanation that the Defence has not been given enough time. We'll continue. Mr. Karadzic, let's upload that document. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, I don't mean to interrupt, I don't have the transcript in front of me, but my recollection is that that topic did come up yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- of the film and this would have been one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's leave it at that, and then why don't we upload that document Mr. Karadzic was referring to. Do you have the 65 ter number, Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I do not have it at my finger tips, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only have the ERN number 06054891, 19 August, 1998, a report on the interview with Mr. Rutten. I believe it's a report from the OTP, the Prosecution. 2247, a Prosecution exhibit. Your Excellencies, with all due respect, it's not only that we are short of time. We have inadequate resources, inadequate personnel. If everybody recognises that this is a mega-trial, our resources are not mega. They are substandard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unacceptable, Mr. Karadzic. Have we found that document? So why don't we proceed without the document and we'll come back to that issue later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, it's 22457, we found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we now waiting for the document or are we moving on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's coming.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This passage is on page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, I'll read it in Serbian: "First, I spoke to Mr. De Ruiter and then with Commander Bleumink. De Ruiter told me that something horrendous had happened. He spoke for a lot, but briefly because Mr. Bleumink took over and he said video footage has more implications than we had initially expected. I could only think that what was said was true. I was asked what it was about. I was asked not to speak about it because we were all required to obey the rule of not divulging information. I said, 'No need to tell me this. I have no vested interest in this.' They can't go any further into this subject." Can you see what is written below? The next day, they told him, in a dramatic tone, that the footage had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of that? And if you were not, how come these things were happening without your knowledge, although you held such a high position?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: First, I was not in such a high office; second, the rolls of film were not delivered to me and I was not involved in the entire process, only, let's say, going off to take pictures. I did consult with Rutten about that and I indicated something unusual happened in that region, it might be a good idea to record it in photographs, I remember that, but after that I wasn't involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There's no basis to admit this document at the moment. I think this could have been the first document you could have put to the witness when Mr. Rutten was here instead of delving into background material.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just, Your Honours, I mean it's clear what's going on here. Obviously the Defence read through all of Mr. Rutten's statements before they cross-examined him. It's hard to believe that in preparation for Colonel Boering, after Rutten finished, they went back and read Rutten's statements and then came up with this question for the first time. I mean, I think it's a clear tactical choice when Mr. Rutten said yesterday that the film was destroyed by an error, I'm paraphrasing, in the development, they chose not to put this question to him because they didn't want to get the answer from the witness himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, that's absolutely not the case and the case is, in fact, that Dr. Karadzic discovered this last night and that's how chaos -- that's a product of chaos and that's what we have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Whatever the consequence of that chaos would be, there's no basis to admit this document through this witness, so we'll not admit this, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, I ask you to re-call Mr. Rutten for me to finish my cross-examination or to admit this through a bar table motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a separate subject. Let's get on with the -- get on with your cross-examination of Mr. Boering.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 11th of July, 1995, around 8.00 p.m. you had your first meeting with General Mladic at the Fontana Hotel; correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was your position regarding the civilians in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: My role was to serve as a point of contact, both with the civilian population and the military leadership in the enclave. That's why I was in touch with civilian -- civilian institutions in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry, I may have been imprecise. You were there as a team, right, and you were led by the battalion commander, Mr. Karremans. There was also Mr. -- sorry, Major Raven and Mr. Rave and others. What was the position of your side, not your personal position, what did you come to Mladic with?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The enclave had fallen. The Muslim population was in a dire situation, and the idea was to see what the best way was to find a solution for this with the VRS. At that moment it was unclear whether we would find Mladic there. We wanted to meet to find possible solutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you come up with a proposal? Did you have a view?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The view we had was primarily that of the Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans. At that moment the situation was fairly chaotic. True joint preparation as a team as to how we would act together -- I don't remember preparing that in detail in writing or otherwise, except for a brief talk beforehand, but that was more about consulting with the other side and exploring options there because the idea of truly negotiating was not really present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you informed of the operation of the action undertaken that morning by Ambassador Akashi regarding Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: No, I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you keep each other informed? Did you collate information with your centre in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I wasn't involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If your commander was involved, would it be reasonable for me to assume that you had briefings? Did you have briefings to be informed about orders and other information coming from your command?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: We had regular briefings and often we would get together for an hour in the early evening to review various matters in a small group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the reason for your failure to come up with proposal the fact that Mladic had asked you to bring representatives of the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: Did any proposal or conclusion come out of that first meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that General Mladic indicated that he wanted to consult with Muslims from the enclave, preferably military ones. And he wanted that to happen that very night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you returned the same night, around 11.00 p.m.; right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the conclusion of that second meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: The conclusion of the second meeting, if I remember correctly, was an appointment to meet a third time the next morning, where we made or where we were supposed to make another attempt to try to get a broader composition of the team to elaborate things together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that Mladic informed you that he had neither the buses nor the fuel to evacuate the civilians and he asked the UN to provide them?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: At the third meeting there in Fontana, that came up, transport and buses. I was next to that, so I didn't hear everything. This was one of the areas that was unclear between Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans and myself. That's why I returned again after the third meeting, after our consultation, to verify what the actual agreements were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. By that time it was clear to you, wasn't it, that Muslim representatives were asking you to facilitate the evacuation of civilians; right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: At the third meeting we spoke about a certain procedure for removing the Muslim population based on age categories, for example, first the sick and the injured; and afterwards, those who were more mobile. Those matters came up at the third meeting. Even DutchBat's support in this removal came up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who asked for the removal? Whose position was it that they want evacuation?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I remember that there were -- the situation was very bleak for the population and for the battalion that I was a member of. I don't remember -- I don't remember whether the actual initiative came from the battalion or the Muslim population or General Mladic at the third meeting. There was talk about that being possible and how, but the initiative, I think that wasn't clearly stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see 65 ter 02367. It's probably been admitted already, so there's probably a P number as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P3974, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can remove the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this telegram sent by your commander?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I saw this telegram afterwards, but obviously not during the operation itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at paragraph 4, what the demands were, that by 2230 another meeting be held and the meeting was to be attended by representatives of all refugees. Quote: "I found one, although he was not an official representative ...," et cetera, et cetera. And he said the cease-fire would last until 10.00 on the 12th of July. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I can see only the first part of the page. Could I see the second part? Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He agreed to accept all the humanitarian needs of the refugees, to admit all the wounded, et cetera, but his conditions were that soldiers, Muslim soldiers, be disarmed and that they withdraw. And we see that he was willing to receive and treat all wounded persons, et cetera. Was it, indeed, so?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Do you mean whether General Mladic indicated this orally; is that what you're asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, is this report by Karremans correct? Did you attend these meetings with Mr. Karremans?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, I was present there. And as for whether this came up, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we scroll down the page to see item 6, what Mr. Karremans says he was not able to do. Please look at this. He says he cannot defend these people, he cannot defend his own battalion, he cannot find suitable representatives of the civilians and their authorities, he cannot find representatives among the military authorities because they are trying to fight for a corridor to the Tuzla area, and he cannot manage to force the ABiH army to hand over their weapons. Was it indeed the situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D4883.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is from General Gobillard. It's a telegram sent to the north-east sector, I suppose. It's an order issued to DutchBat. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I didn't see those telegrams at the time. I wasn't involved in that. Well, it was clear that different levels were in contact with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This order - it is entitled "Order," isn't it? - was it carried out by your forces? Did you act accordingly?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: You're talking about my troops. I wasn't the commander. I was a staff officer and was responsible for contact between different parties. So I was involved in the process but not actually as a type of commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, all right, sir, Mr. Boering. You are testifying here about everything that has to do with Serbs. Can you testify about anything that has to do with your battalion? Also, you're not testifying only about your contacts with the parties; you're testifying about different things here. Was this carried out? Did your commander behave in accordance with this order?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, just let me take a look for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we zoom in further that second part, starting from the message.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, from what I see, that is, indeed, how we operated on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1958, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 19460, could we have that 65 ter number now, please. We're going to get the English version now as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this. Is this telegram being sent by the General Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the 1st Corps command and to the president of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina at 1325 hours on the 12th of July; isn't that right? P3981 is the number of this document, actually. It has already been admitted. You don't have to read all of it. I'm just asking you whether you agree that this was sent on the 12th of July at 1.25.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I see a sheet of paper bearing a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the first paragraph. Do you agree that what it says here is that he is already acting on the instructions that he had received in order to prepare for accepting a large number of civilians from Srebrenica? It's the first paragraph. Do you agree that that is what it says there?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: That's what I'm reading, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this now, Mr. Boering: Do you know that the Muslim side had consulted Mr. Akashi and that Mr. Akashi, on the 11th, said that he would start talks with the Serb side on the basis of the consultations held with the Muslim side in order to ensure the evacuation of civilians from Srebrenica. Now, take a look at this. Already on the 12th, this one is providing information to the effect that he is acting upon instructions to receive these civilians, and Akashi says after consultations with the Muslim side he is going to talk to the Serb side to make this possible. Did you know about all of this?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: No, I knew nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know about Akashi's telegram to the Secretary-General and to Annan?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: No, I knew nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you see for yourself that the representatives of Muslims from Srebrenica were asking for the evacuation of the civilian population to be facilitated, that this was their request, and that all of that was in full accord. On the 11th, it was the government -- is talking to Akashi and sending instructions to this -- this -- this 2nd Corps, the 2nd Corps -- the 2nd Corps is already providing information on the 12th, in the afternoon, that they had taken measures. Now, who was it that asked for the population to be evacuated, Mr. Boering?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: If you're talking about the representatives of the Muslim population in the enclave, then Mandzic, Camila and Mr. Nuhanovic, they had actual ideas about requesting evacuation. I remember that in the previous night they were consulting and making phone calls, trying to contact various authorities in Tuzla. But advance instructions or plans, whether they had those, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 65 ter 19713.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this? Is this the usual telegram that is sent by HQ Sector North East and the Tuzla Airbase?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I can't remember having seen such cover sheets very often. It's possible. It looks authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this. The date is the 7th of July - isn't that right? - and this has to do with an assessment of the situation in Srebrenica. It says that the Drina Corps has a strength of 11.000 and that it is responsible for the separation line or confrontation line of 90 kilometres and that it is so thinly spread that it is unable to launch an offensive or attack; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at what it says in respect of the 2nd Corps. It says the 2nd Corps, the 2nd Corps: [In English] "It is well -- 2nd Corps is well aware of the BSA problems and would like to exacerbate it by making 28th Division more active. It is worthy of note that the ABiH within Srebrenica and Zepa, although poorly armed, are probably not that much less in number than the total number of the infantry of Drina Corps." [Interpretation] Was that what you knew as well, that they have almost as many soldiers as the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: No, I did not have that impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at what it says here further on. It says that 65 per cent of the required food was allowed to enter and that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was making entrance very difficult and that at least one convoy returned to Belgrade. And a bit further down there's a reference to Oric, that he's in Tuzla. Did you know that? Did you know that he had left Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us please take a look at the next page now. Look at what it says here about Oric, that he treats Srebrenica as his personal fief and [In English] "he is an embarrassment to the BH government as he is suspected of being a war criminal." [Interpretation] Did you know what Naser Oric's forces had done to Serbs in Srebrenica and around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I was aware that there were regular activities outside the enclave by soldiers of the ABiH and also that some people within the enclave were enriching themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see that Muslims attacks Vis, and further on you see what the Army of Republika Srpska did, they start an attack, and it says the local mayor said that he did not believe that the Army of the Bosnian Serbs wished to take the enclave but, rather, they were after strategic hilltops, and so on and so forth. Did you see for yourself that the 28th Division was more active from mid-June up until these days?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I remember that the tension mounted around that time and that freedom of movement, even for us to drive around, became more limited and that here and there there was some joint actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is convenient, Mr. Karadzic, we would like to take a break now --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- for 15 minutes and we'll resume at 11.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we proceed, before I forget again, Mr. Robinson, with respect to your request for leave to reply in relation to the motion to compel the interview, your leave is granted, since the Chamber finds that it would be useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So did you realise what the intensity and volume of this enhanced activity of the 28th Division was in the second half of June? You said that you did know about some operations. Were you aware of the intensity and volume of these military operations from the enclave? At your daily briefings, was this being communicated to your command staff?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, our insight into the operations of the 28th Division, especially operations outside the enclave, was limited, especially because we were heavily restricted in our actions due to lack of personnel, fuel. Often, we were informed of activities outside the enclave by the Muslims reported primarily, for example, by Major Momir Nikolic of [as interpreted] Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was my next question, but you've already answered it. Did you take that seriously, the information that was provided to you by the Serb officers who liaised with you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, Colonel Boering. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, no objection, but just for the transcript being clear on line 38, 2, I think it's meant to be "Nikolic or Vukovic," not "of," as though that was a place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it "of" to be Dutch.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel Boering.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course we took the information seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D04727, please. Can we have a look at that, please. Can we have that in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you are minded to tender the previous document UNMO's document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sorry, I thought that I already did that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1959, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see this? Do you see what is being ordered by Rasim Delic on the 11th of July, Rasim Delic, the Commander-in-Chief of the Muslim army? This is what he says in the preamble: "With a view to intensifying partisan types of combat actions, active actions, and particularly combat action diversions, I hereby order: "Up to the 15th of July, 1995, in the basic zone of operation carry out all preparations for execution of diversion actions at the level of divisions and brigades ..." And then further on what should be done, these operations should be carried out as soon as possible and as often as possible on taken territory, and the basic actions are to be of the destroy-and-come-back type. Do you realise that that was done even before this order?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: In the time I was in the enclave, it happened regularly, at least according to the VRS liaison officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1960, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D4704, can we have a look at that, please. Yes, that's it. You can remove the Serbian version so that there will be more room for the English version -- oh, no, actually for the sake of the public, you can keep both, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see this here, information on combat results of the units and commands of the 28th Army Division of the 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zepa. It's the 8th of July. Please take a look at this. Do you see what they did and to what extent? I'll read out the first one: "The soldiers of the 28th Ground Army Division located in Srebrenica and Zepa, although completely encircled and facing major problems related to survival and the obligation to protect free territory, decided to contribute as much as possible to the fight against the aggressor and stepped up their activities deep in the temporarily taken territory. An additional reason for the activities of the members of the 28th Division was to prevent enemy forces from sending additional troops to the Sarajevo theatre of operations from the area around Srebrenica and Zepa by causing losses, primarily the loss of manpower, which would force the aggressor to tie-up troops in the wider area of Srebrenica and Zepa." And then it says here: "60 Chetniks were liquidated ...," a certain amount of equipment was seized and then the village of Visnjica, you probably know that it's outside the enclave, and so on and so forth. Does this correspond to your own knowledge about their activities in our territory, deep in our territory?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: We were informed in very limited ways about that. We didn't know very much about that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you notice that the activities of the 28th Division had to do with the activities of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina around Sarajevo, and that these activities were reinforced in order to spread out Serb forces? Is this understandable military logic at that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, it's definitely logical. Whether there was the link described here -- well, I can imagine that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1961, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have a look at 1D04729.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know who Ramiz Becirovic was?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, I was regularly in contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was he acting commander of the 28th Division when Naser Oric was absent?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Generally, yes, but possibly with the exception of the Bandera triangle, where Zulfo was effectively in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll go back to the Bandera triangle. Please focus on this now, this is the beginning of June, the 5th of June, and what is referred to here is taking measures to prepare for sabotage activities and it is an order that he is issuing to these brigades. The 282nd and the 283rd, to establish a joint sabotage reconnaissance group that they would send to territory temporarily occupied by the aggressor along the axis Podravanje-Kragljivoda-Jezero. You can see all of this for yourself. And carrying out this task, et cetera, et cetera, they will be able to carry out this activity as soon as they have a chance, and so on and so forth. Do you see that that is the intensive activity that started already in the first days of the month of June?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit D1962.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at 65 ter 19471, please, so that we can see what was happening, what kind of activities were taking place in April when you were there. You were there then; right?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, I was there in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you were ordered to halt the engineering works at your observation points?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Just a moment. Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the reason for banning the fortification of your observation posts was because they wanted to pass between Srebrenica and Zepa unimpeded? That's what it says in the paragraph but last.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, it was important for unimpeded passage to be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that pursuant to the agreement on protected areas, they did not have the right to link-up those two enclaves and that that belt of the territory, that road, was supposed to have been under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, in any case, I do remember that those two enclaves were not connected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you recall, do you agree, did you have information that helicopters with weapons preferred to land in Zepa rather than in Srebrenica, and that then these weapons were taken from Zepa to Srebrenica later via this corridor?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: No, I don't have my information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you did have information about helicopter landings, did you not, and even about us downing or firing at those helicopters?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Yes, but that related to helicopters intending to land in the Srebrenica enclave, especially in the dark a few times. Such reports were made, but I didn't personally see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you report the hostile position of the 2nd Corps command and of the 28th Division towards the UNPROFOR? Did you inform your superiors about this?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: That was not part of my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the battalion report about it? Was it something that could be found in the media? Was the command in Zagreb and Sarajevo informed about it? And was this given out to the media, all that was being done to you in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, there was standard reports about what was happening in and around the enclave - DutchBat drafted them - so anything noteworthy was reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was that reported to the media? Were there any protests through the media about these hostile actions?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I don't remember reports to the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would like to tender this --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, while the document is still on the screen, do you see that there is reference here to the demilitarisation agreement. When it is useful or needed, then there was reference to the demilitarisation agreement. Was the Srebrenica area ever demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: One of our duties was to carry that out, and we were able to implement that in a very limited manner.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Exhibit D1963.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 19472, these --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit P3990, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And since probably this document was tendered through you, did you see this document during your preparation for this testimony?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I didn't see this document in my preparation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at paragraph 3, where it says: [In English] "The attempt made by the liaison officer of the 28th Army Division to prevent UNPROFOR in Srebrenica from continuing its work to set up an observation station in the village of Lozine sector by citing the Agreement on the Cessation of Hostilities on 31st of December, 1994, was erroneous because this is exactly what the Agreement envisages." [Interpretation] Do you recall inheriting - you came immediately after that - the cease-fire that was mediated by President Carter and signed on the 31st of December, shortly before you arrived?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 65 ter 01979, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Muslim side painted its APCs white in order for them to look like your APCs? Were you informed about that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: When I was in the enclave, I didn't see any APCs of the Muslims, let alone painted ones -- let alone ones that were painted white.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Take a look at this. This is dated the 8th of July, and it states that the UNPROFOR command filed a protest to the Main Staff of the VRS over operations against UNPROFOR observation point at this elevation near Zeleni Jadar and then the Main Staff responded that the Drina Corps command had informed it that the Muslims were using or misusing six armoured personnel carriers painted white and acting at close range. Do you agree that the Muslims were firing close from your observation points in the near vicinity in order to provoke us to fire back and to break the cease-fire? Not to break the cease-fire but to actually pull UNPROFOR into the war on their side.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: I remember that occasionally there were some Muslim activities near the enclave. I do remember that. And this was discussed with the Muslim military. We said that we did not want to tolerate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said "near the enclave." Did you mean to say that in the near vicinity of your installations they were firing and that that was something that you were not prepared to tolerate?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: Well, in any case our mandate was to act on that, let alone if it happened in our neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Boering, perhaps my question was not clear. Did the Muslims abuse your presence in order to fire against the Serbs from positions that were close to your observation points so that the Serbs would retaliate by firing back at you, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING
utterances.text: This may have happened occasionally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would like to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1964 [Realtime transcript read in error "D1946"], Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not 46 but 64 in the transcript. Let's look at 1D04723.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the final analysis of the air-lift for Zepa and Srebrenica. It was written on the 17th of February, 1995; however, I think that that was an error. I think that this happened in 1996, that there was an error made in the year.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the following page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you look at the place where it says that: "Between the 27th of February, 1993, and the 7th of May, 1995, there was an air-lift from the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to meet the needs of the enclave of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde. The main aim of introducing and maintaining the air-lift was to transport" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's too fast. Slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
